report.incidentSummary: At the 09:15 IST (03:45 UTC) market open on 2026-09-14, approximately 15% of stock orders failed with HTTP 503 after encountering HTTP 429 Too Many Requests from the upstream broker API. The order-service retried up to 3 times before rejecting the orders. A concurrent database CPU spike to ~75% and slow queries were caused by an unrelated traffic surge on portfolio-service querying user holdings, and did not impact order execution as order-service connection pool wait times remained under 5 ms.
report.rootCauseStatement: Surging market open order volume at 09:15 IST exceeded the upstream broker API rate limit quota, causing broker-connector to receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and order-service to reject orders after retries were exhausted.

hypotheses.cause: Market open order volume exceeded upstream broker API rate limits, resulting in HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses and subsequent order rejections after retries exhausted.
hypotheses.rationale: Logs in order-service and broker-connector show hundreds of HTTP 429 Too Many Requests errors and order rejections after retry attempts starting at 03:45 UTC. The broker-connector rate-limited metric surged to over 575/min and error rates peaked at 11.24% while order-service error rates reached 15.53%.

hypotheses.cause: Database CPU saturation and slow holdings queries degraded order-service database connection pool and caused order failures.
hypotheses.rationale: Although database CPU spiked to 75.6% and slow queries surged to 31/min due to portfolio-service traffic on holdings, order-service database pool wait time peaked at only 4.79 ms, showing no connection starvation. Furthermore, all logged order rejections were explicitly status 503 due to upstream broker 429 rate limits, not database timeouts.

facts.statement: Between 03:45 UTC and 04:21 UTC, broker-connector logged 378 occurrences of 'POST /orders -> 429 Too Many Requests' and order-service logged 290 occurrences of 'order rejected: broker rate limit (429) after retries'.
order-service error_rate surged from ~0.4% baseline to 12.52% at 03:45 UTC, peaking at 15.53% at 04:00 UTC before recovering to normal (0.36%) by 04:25 UTC.
broker-connector rate_limited_count spiked from 0 to 353.9/min at 03:45 UTC, peaking at 575.6/min at 04:10 UTC, while its error_rate peaked at 11.24%.
order-service db_pool_wait_ms remained minimal throughout the incident, peaking at 4.79 ms at 03:45 UTC against a normal baseline of 2.4-2.8 ms.

Database cpu_utilization increased from ~37% to 67.3% at 03:45 UTC and peaked at 75.59% at 03:50 UTC, driven by slow queries on 'SELECT ... FROM holdings WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY updated_at' as portfolio-service request rate jumped from 845 to 1605 req/s.
No deployments, configuration changes, or migrations occurred in order-service, database, broker-connector, or portfolio-service during or immediately preceding the incident window.

inferences.statement: The order failures were caused directly by upstream broker rate limits rather than database connection contention or database pool exhaustion.
The database CPU spike was an incidental co-occurring symptom caused by user app open traffic querying portfolio holdings, not the cause of order failures.
The increase in order-service latency_p95_ms (to 532.6 ms) was caused by repeated backoff retry attempts against broker-connector upon encountering 429 status codes.

assumptions.statement: The upstream broker quota breach was driven by genuine open-market order volume from users rather than a rogue internal client or retry storm bug.

timeline.event: Market opens. Portfolio-service request rate jumps to 1605 req/s. Database CPU increases to 67.3%. Broker rate limiting begins with rate_limited_count jumping to 353.9/min.
First logged HTTP 429 Too Many Requests response from broker API.
First order rejection logged in order-service after retries exhausted (status 503).
Database CPU peaks at 75.59%; broker-connector error rate peaks at 11.24%.
order-service error_rate peaks at 15.53%.
broker-connector rate_limited_count reaches peak of 575.6/min.
Broker rate limit errors subside to 28.4/min and order-service error rate drops to 1.1%.
Order-service error rate and broker-connector rate_limited_count return to baseline levels (<0.4%).

confidence.rationale: Log messages and metrics explicitly document HTTP 429 Too Many Requests from the broker API causing order rejections, matching the exact failure window. Metrics rule out database connection delays as the cause of order failures.

gaps.description: Upstream broker API dashboard/contract rate limits were not directly accessible to verify the exact contracted TPS threshold.
gaps.impact: Low; application logs and metric counters definitively show HTTP 429 status codes returned from broker API.

gaps.description: Holdings table indexing and query plans could not be inspected due to tool call budget constraints.
gaps.impact: Low; database CPU spike was proven orthogonal to order rejections.

recommendedActions.action: Coordinate with upstream broker partner to increase order placement TPS / rate limit quotas for the 09:15-09:30 IST market open window.
recommendedActions.rationale: Order burst volume at open consistently hit upstream broker HTTP 429 quotas, leading to rejected client orders.
recommendedActions.verification: Check broker-connector rate_limited_count and 429 error logs during upcoming market open windows.

recommendedActions.action: Implement client-side request pacing / smoothing and dynamic Retry-After backoff in broker-connector to avoid overwhelming the upstream broker API during market open.
recommendedActions.rationale: Bursty open orders trigger immediate broker 429s and rapid retries exacerbate rate limit exhaustion.
recommendedActions.verification: Verify broker-connector honors upstream retry-after headers and queues/paces outbound requests during simulated traffic bursts.

recommendedActions.action: Optimize holdings queries in portfolio-service (e.g. adding index on (user_id, updated_at) or caching holdings summaries) to mitigate database CPU spikes during market open.
recommendedActions.rationale: Slow holdings queries took 1-3 seconds and drove database CPU to 75.6% during market open.
recommendedActions.verification: Observe database slow_queries_per_min and cpu_utilization at 09:15 IST after index/caching deployment.

report.justification: The investigation stopped without critic review due to reaching planned completion. The evidence conclusively proves the root cause: broker-connector received HTTP 429 responses directly from the upstream broker API (recorded in both logs and metric counters), while database pool wait times remained under 5 ms, directly refuting the initial database CPU suspicion.

payload.markdown:
# Investigation report: Orders erroring at the open

**Outcome:** conclusive · **Stop reason:** completed · **Confidence:** 0.90 · **Written by:** reporting agent

## Summary
At the 09:15 IST (03:45 UTC) market open on 2026-09-14, approximately 15% of stock orders failed with HTTP 503 after encountering HTTP 429 Too Many Requests from the upstream broker API. The order-service retried up to 3 times before rejecting the orders. A concurrent database CPU spike to ~75% and slow queries were caused by an unrelated traffic surge on portfolio-service querying user holdings, and did not impact order execution as order-service connection pool wait times remained under 5 ms.

**Root cause:** Surging market open order volume at 09:15 IST exceeded the upstream broker API rate limit quota, causing broker-connector to receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and order-service to reject orders after retries were exhausted.

## Hypotheses
1. **Market open order volume exceeded upstream broker API rate limits, resulting in HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses and subsequent order rejections after retries exhausted.** — `broker-connector`, rate_limiting_or_quota, confidence 0.90, supported
   - Supporting: [ev_2, ev_10, ev_11, ev_12, ev_14, ev_16] · Contradicting: none
   - Logs in order-service and broker-connector show hundreds of HTTP 429 Too Many Requests errors and order rejections after retry attempts starting at 03:45 UTC. The broker-connector rate-limited metric surged to over 575/min and error rates peaked at 11.24% while order-service error rates reached 15.53%.
2. **Database CPU saturation and slow holdings queries degraded order-service database connection pool and caused order failures.** — `database`, capacity_saturation, confidence 0.05, ruled_out
   - Supporting: [ev_1, ev_5, ev_15, ev_17, ev_18] · Contradicting: [ev_2, ev_4, ev_11]
   - Although database CPU spiked to 75.6% and slow queries surged to 31/min due to portfolio-service traffic on holdings, order-service database pool wait time peaked at only 4.79 ms, showing no connection starvation. Furthermore, all logged order rejections were explicitly status 503 due to upstream broker 429 rate limits, not database timeouts.

## Facts
- Between 03:45 UTC and 04:21 UTC, broker-connector logged 378 occurrences of 'POST /orders -> 429 Too Many Requests' and order-service logged 290 occurrences of 'order rejected: broker rate limit (429) after retries'. [ev_2, ev_11]
- order-service error_rate surged from ~0.4% baseline to 12.52% at 03:45 UTC, peaking at 15.53% at 04:00 UTC before recovering to normal (0.36%) by 04:25 UTC. [ev_10]
- broker-connector rate_limited_count spiked from 0 to 353.9/min at 03:45 UTC, peaking at 575.6/min at 04:10 UTC, while its error_rate peaked at 11.24%. [ev_14, ev_16]
- order-service db_pool_wait_ms remained minimal throughout the incident, peaking at 4.79 ms at 03:45 UTC against a normal baseline of 2.4-2.8 ms. [ev_4]
- Database cpu_utilization increased from ~37% to 67.3% at 03:45 UTC and peaked at 75.59% at 03:50 UTC, driven by slow queries on 'SELECT ... FROM holdings WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY updated_at' as portfolio-service request rate jumped from 845 to 1605 req/s. [ev_5, ev_15, ev_17, ev_18]
- No deployments, configuration changes, or migrations occurred in order-service, database, broker-connector, or portfolio-service during or immediately preceding the incident window. [ev_3, ev_7]

## Inferences
- The order failures were caused directly by upstream broker rate limits rather than database connection contention or database pool exhaustion. [ev_2, ev_4, ev_10, ev_11, ev_14, ev_16]
- The database CPU spike was an incidental co-occurring symptom caused by user app open traffic querying portfolio holdings, not the cause of order failures. [ev_4, ev_5, ev_15, ev_18]
- The increase in order-service latency_p95_ms (to 532.6 ms) was caused by repeated backoff retry attempts against broker-connector upon encountering 429 status codes. [ev_2, ev_11, ev_12]

## Assumptions
- The upstream broker quota breach was driven by genuine open-market order volume from users rather than a rogue internal client or retry storm bug.

## Timeline
- **2026-09-14 09:15 IST (03:45:00 UTC)** Market opens. Portfolio-service request rate jumps to 1605 req/s. Database CPU increases to 67.3%. Broker rate limiting begins with rate_limited_count jumping to 353.9/min. [ev_14, ev_15, ev_18]
- **2026-09-14 09:15:05 IST (03:45:05 UTC)** First logged HTTP 429 Too Many Requests response from broker API. [ev_2]
- **2026-09-14 09:15:32 IST (03:45:32 UTC)** First order rejection logged in order-service after retries exhausted (status 503). [ev_2, ev_11]
- **2026-09-14 09:20 IST (03:50:00 UTC)** Database CPU peaks at 75.59%; broker-connector error rate peaks at 11.24%. [ev_15, ev_16]
- **2026-09-14 09:30 IST (04:00:00 UTC)** order-service error_rate peaks at 15.53%. [ev_10]
- **2026-09-14 09:40 IST (04:10:00 UTC)** broker-connector rate_limited_count reaches peak of 575.6/min. [ev_14]
- **2026-09-14 09:50 IST (04:20:00 UTC)** Broker rate limit errors subside to 28.4/min and order-service error rate drops to 1.1%. [ev_10, ev_14]
- **2026-09-14 09:55 IST (04:25:00 UTC)** Order-service error rate and broker-connector rate_limited_count return to baseline levels (<0.4%). [ev_10, ev_14]

## Confidence
0.90: Log messages and metrics explicitly document HTTP 429 Too Many Requests from the broker API causing order rejections, matching the exact failure window. Metrics rule out database connection delays as the cause of order failures.

## Gaps
- Upstream broker API dashboard/contract rate limits were not directly accessible to verify the exact contracted TPS threshold. (impact: Low; application logs and metric counters definitively show HTTP 429 status codes returned from broker API.)
- Holdings table indexing and query plans could not be inspected due to tool call budget constraints. (impact: Low; database CPU spike was proven orthogonal to order rejections.)

## Recommended actions (not executed)
- **[now]** Coordinate with upstream broker partner to increase order placement TPS / rate limit quotas for the 09:15-09:30 IST market open window. [ev_2, ev_14]
  - Why: Order burst volume at open consistently hit upstream broker HTTP 429 quotas, leading to rejected client orders.
  - Verify: Check broker-connector rate_limited_count and 429 error logs during upcoming market open windows.
- **[next]** Implement client-side request pacing / smoothing and dynamic Retry-After backoff in broker-connector to avoid overwhelming the upstream broker API during market open. [ev_2, ev_11]
  - Why: Bursty open orders trigger immediate broker 429s and rapid retries exacerbate rate limit exhaustion.
  - Verify: Verify broker-connector honors upstream retry-after headers and queues/paces outbound requests during simulated traffic bursts.
- **[next]** Optimize holdings queries in portfolio-service (e.g. adding index on (user_id, updated_at) or caching holdings summaries) to mitigate database CPU spikes during market open. [ev_5, ev_15, ev_17, ev_18]
  - Why: Slow holdings queries took 1-3 seconds and drove database CPU to 75.6% during market open.
  - Verify: Observe database slow_queries_per_min and cpu_utilization at 09:15 IST after index/caching deployment.

## Justification
The investigation stopped without critic review due to reaching planned completion. The evidence conclusively proves the root cause: broker-connector received HTTP 429 responses directly from the upstream broker API (recorded in both logs and metric counters), while database pool wait times remained under 5 ms, directly refuting the initial database CPU suspicion.
